summary: MaRaBeTha is an interactive 3D globe that tests 30 Earth-science hypotheses against long-term NASA satellite records. Each region tells a story: the Amazon and Ganges river mouths, Lake Chad, the Aral Sea, the Amazon Arc of Deforestation, the Greenland Ice Sheet, the Great Barrier Reef and others. They are grouped into four themes: coastal estuaries, water stress, forests and land use, and the cryosphere and atmosphere. For each region we state what we expect to happen to a variable such as chlorophyll-a, soil moisture, land surface temperature or NO₂. A Python pipeline collects monthly series from NASA Giovanni and AppEEARS, then runs a Mann-Kendall test corrected for autocorrelation, along with Sen’s slope and its 95% confidence interval. Each hypothesis ends up confirmed, contradicted, inconclusive or lacking data. The challenge asks for exactly this: a variable, a specific region, a long time series, a rate of change and a significance test. Our app makes the whole chain readable by non-specialists. It shows not only whether a place is changing, but whether that change is statistically real and what it means, and an AI assistant answers questions about the numbers on screen.
details:
What it does. Users spin a 3D globe and open one of 30 study regions. Each region opens as a story in chapters: the place, the hypothesis, the evidence, “Is it real?”, what it means, and where to explore next. The evidence chapter shows the monthly satellite series with Sen’s trend line. “Is it real?” shows the corrected Mann-Kendall p-value, Kendall’s τ, the 95% confidence interval of Sen’s slope, the number of months, data completeness and the effective number of independent months. Each series also gets a data-quality grade (ready, use with caution, exploratory only, insufficient), so a gap-filled series is never shown as a solid result. Some stories contrast two regions with opposite outcomes, for example a dammed delta against a free-flowing river.

How it works.

  1. Collectors pull monthly series from NASA Giovanni and NASA AppEEARS (MODIS) for each region’s bounding boxes and store them in Supabase.
  2. trend-analysis (Python) runs Mann-Kendall with an AR(1) autocorrelation correction, Sen’s slope with confidence intervals, and completeness checks. It then gives each hypothesis a verdict and writes a versioned JSON report.
  3. trend-api (Python) computes a region’s analysis live from the database when a story opens, starts new data collections, and serves an AI agent (“Ask the data”) that answers questions with the region’s real numbers as context.
  4. The Next.js front end renders the globe and stories. It passes the agent the exact numbers the user is looking at, so a question like “what does this 16.7% mean?” gets a grounded answer.

Benefits and intended impact. Climate and land-use trends are often reported as headlines without uncertainty. MaRaBeTha shows the test and its caveats next to every claim, including when the data says “we can’t tell yet.” We want students, journalists, educators and policymakers to learn the habit of asking whether a trend is statistically real before trusting it. Anyone can also reuse the method on new regions and variables.

Tools and languages. TypeScript, Next.js 16, React 19, react-globe.gl and three.js on the front end, deployed on Vercel. Python for data collection, statistics and the API, hosted on Render, with Supabase (Postgres) for storage. Data comes from NASA Giovanni, NASA AppEEARS (MODIS) and NASA Blue Marble textures, with Natural Earth outlines and Wikimedia Commons photos credited under their licenses. An LLM agent (Gemini) powers the Q&A. The design was done in Figma, and GitLab and GitHub were used for collaboration.

The user can access: https://spaceappschallenge-tau.vercel.app
Our code is hosted in: https://gitlab.com/marabetha

Creativity. Instead of a dashboard, every region is a scientific investigation told as a story. The hypothesis comes first, the data second, and the verdict can be “contradicted,” so the app shows that science is allowed to be wrong. Regions are paired so that human pressure (dams, irrigation, urbanization) can be read against natural variability. The assistant knows what is on the user’s screen, so it explains the actual numbers rather than giving general answers.

Factors we considered.

  • Statistics: monthly satellite series are seasonal and autocorrelated, so we chose non-parametric tests and corrected for autocorrelation instead of relying on a naive regression.
  • Data gaps: a minimum of 36 valid months is required, and completeness is shown.
  • Honest labels: sample or demo data is always labelled as such.
  • Reliability: the API has rate limits and retries, and API keys never reach the browser.
  • Attribution: image licenses are credited.
